newsitem.title: UK: London gold dips, then bounces after U.S. jobs.
newsitem.headline: London gold dips, then bounces after U.S. jobs.

text.p: Gold prices were barely changed on Friday afternoon following stronger-than-expected U.S. monthly jobs data announced midday.
Bullion fixed at $385.40 an ounce, compared to $385.60 in the morning. Prices remained below Thursday's London close of $386.10/$386.60 amid overall bearish sentiment.
The market's initial reaction to the jobs data, which pointed to continued strong economic growth, was a brief dip to the day's low, with a bid quoted at $384.80.
"The market's first reaction was to think stronger interest rates. But then support came in under $385.50," a dealer said.
U.S. non-farm payrolls rose 250,000 from a gain of 228,000 the previous month. The unemployment rate was 5.1 percent, the lowest since March, 1989, compared to 5.4 previously.
Dealers were mixed as to whether the data were bullish or bearish for gold. The bond market and the dollar initially dropped, then rallied after the data were released.
"It's pretty disappointing because the figures were strong, which means inflation, which is good for gold," one said.
But the threat of rising U.S. interest rates would diminish gold's appeal to investors, thereby counterbalancing any bullish effect of inflationary pressure, others said.
The market will have to shake itself out of seasonal lull before investors start paying attention to gold, analysts said.
"There is a significant absence of interest on the part of investors to gold now," said analyst Kevin Crisp of JP Morgan.
"Clearly if we start getting more evidence of the potential for rising inflation, we'll get more people getting interested in gold. But it's too early," Crisp said.

Technical analysts said gold was running into trouble on the charts. Analyst Elli Gifford of Investment Research of Cambridge noted that a positive "rounding base" formation for gold was starting to look improbable.
"Support is under test -- if it breaks, that formation can be forgotten," Gifford said in a commentary.
Silver was still down after Thursday's New York-based fund selling, indicated three cents lower at $5.16/$5.18. Dealers said it may be vulerable to more losses.
Platinum was indicated at $393.50/$394.50, off $0.40. It was off lows -- the low bid so far was quoted at $391.50 -- but still in danger of further easing in view of a lack of interest.
